intro: To change canvas size in Photoshop on Mac, open Image > Canvas Size or press Option+Command+C (⌥⌘C). Enter the new width and height, pick an anchor point and an extension color, then click OK.
tldr: Open Image > Canvas Size, or press Option+Command+C, to change the frame around your picture.
Canvas Size changes the workspace. Image > Image Size scales the pixels, so pick the right command.
Pick the anchor square first. It decides which side of the photo the new space lands on.
If the extension color is greyed out, the image has no Background layer. Use Layer > New > Background from Layer.
The web app has no dedicated Canvas Size command. Use the Crop tool under Size & position instead.

blocks.text: Canvas Size changes the frame around your picture. It does not scale the picture. Use it when you need more room on one side, a border around the edge, or a smaller frame that trims the edges. If you only need a smaller file, this is the wrong command.
Canvas size vs Image Size in Photoshop on Mac

The command sits in the Image menu, close to Image Size. The two names sound alike, but they do different jobs. Canvas Size changes the workspace. The pixels inside the picture keep their size, and new space appears around them. Image Size changes the pixels themselves, so the photo gets bigger or smaller.

rows: The frame. Pixels keep their size.
Room for text, borders or a trimmed frame
Making the photo itself larger or smaller
Previews the frame and can extend it unevenly
Framing by eye, with fill options
blocks.caption: Three ways to change the frame, and what each one touches.

blocks.text: Use Canvas Size when the photo is right and the frame is wrong. Use Image Size when the photo itself must change size. If you are unsure, look at the edges before you save. Stretched faces or squashed products tell you that you picked the wrong command.
Canvas extension color greyed out: check the Background layer
Photoshop treats the Background layer differently from other layers. Open Window > Layers to see the stack. A Background layer has a small lock icon and sits at the bottom of the stack.

The lock matters in two cases. A missing Background layer can grey out the extension color option. A locked Background also blocks a transparent border, because the new area needs an unlocked layer to show transparency. Check this first, and the rest of the steps go smoothly.
The Canvas Size dialog, field by field
The dialog is short. Five parts control the result. Learn what each one does, and the command stops feeling like guesswork.

items: Unit dropdown: Percent, Pixels, Centimeters or Millimeters. Choose this first.
Width and Height: the final size, unless Relative is ticked.
Relative checkbox: unticked by default. Ticked, it adds or subtracts a set amount.
Anchor grid: nine squares. The square you pick sets where the image sits.
Canvas extension color: White by default, plus Grey, Black and Other.

blocks.text: Canvas Size does not preview anything. You type, click OK, and then check. That is why a quick undo is part of the normal workflow. If you want to see the result before you commit, the Crop tool is the better option.
Worked example: room for a headline on one side
Say you have a portrait and want clean space on the right for a headline. Open Canvas Size. Leave Relative unticked, then type a width larger than the current width. Keep the height the same.

Now click the middle-left square in the anchor grid. The photo stays on the left, and all the new width lands on the right. Keep White as the extension color, then click OK. Check the edge before you add any text.
Keep the headline on its own text layer, so you can move it without touching the photo.
Transparent border in Photoshop on Mac, not a solid color

A transparent border helps with logos, stickers and images for web pages with a colored background. Start by clearing the lock on the Background layer. Click its lock icon in the Layers panel. Then run Canvas Size and choose the new size.

The new area shows a checkerboard pattern. That pattern means transparent, not white. Save as PNG if you want to keep the transparency. JPEG cannot keep transparency, so the border gets a solid color.
Fill the new area with color or generated content

For a plain color fill, pick a color in Canvas Size. For a fill after the fact, use the Paint Bucket tool on the new area. The Paint Bucket needs a layer that accepts paint, so a locked Background gets in the way. Click the lock icon first, the same step that makes transparency possible.

The Crop tool offers three fill options: Default, Content-Aware Fill and Generative Expand. Content-Aware Fill builds the new area from nearby pixels. Generative Expand uses generative AI to extend the scene. If the Crop tool gives odd patches, Content-Aware is selected. Deselect it in the options bar.
Crop tool as an alternative to Canvas Size

Press C to choose the Crop tool. Drag the handles outside the image to extend the canvas. The Crop tool previews the result before you commit. It can extend one side more than another, so check every edge before you press Return.
Pick a unit for print or screen before you type

Decide the unit before you type anything. Pixels suit screens, because a screen has a fixed pixel size. Centimeters or Millimeters suit a print with a set size. Percent scales from the current frame, so it works well for quick, proportional changes.
Clipped pixels when you shrink the canvas

Shrinking the canvas cuts away the edges. Photoshop warns you first, with Proceed, Learn More and Cancel. Choose Cancel if you are not sure what gets lost. Save a copy of the file before you shrink it.

If you might need the cut edges later, use the Crop tool and untick Delete Cropped Pixels in the options bar. The cropped pixels stay in the file outside the visible frame, so you can bring them back.
Shortcut confusion: Option+Command+C or Shift+Command+C?

Most guides give Option+Command+C for Canvas Size on Mac. One guide, updated in September 2022, gives Shift+Command+C. The two conflict. Adobe's own shortcut page could not be checked for this page, so treat both as unconfirmed.
The safest route is the menu. Open the Image menu and read the shortcut printed next to Canvas Size in your copy of Photoshop. Use the printed shortcut, because menus can change between builds.
Photoshop on the web: canvas size options

The web app is a separate tool with fewer controls. Adobe's free online Photoshop page describes uploads of JPEG, JPG or PNG files up to 40MB. Files can be no larger than 8,000 by 8,000 pixels, and you upload one file at a time. The page does not describe canvas or image size controls.

An Adobe Community answer from November 2023 says there is no dedicated Canvas Size command on the web. It suggests the Crop tool under Size & position. Drag the crop handles outside the image, or type width and height values. That answer is user-written, so check the menus in your browser first.
Which version of Photoshop you need

Adobe's release coverage says Photoshop 27.0 came out on October 28, 2025. Photoshop 27.6 followed on April 28, 2026. Both need macOS 14.0 or later. If you are not sure which build you have, [check your Photoshop version](/how-to/check-your-photoshop-version-in-photoshop).

The steps on this page come from third-party guides. Adobe's own help pages could not be checked for this page. The main guide was written from Photoshop CC on Windows, and its sources did not show a Mac-specific change to the dialog. The screenshots may look a little different on your Mac, so the fields and the anchor grid are the parts to watch.
Common mistakes that waste time

One common mistake is using Image Size by accident. Another is choosing the wrong anchor square. A third is picking a unit you did not mean. A value typed in Percent makes a very different frame than the same number typed in Pixels.

Another mistake is trusting the first look. Canvas Size gives no preview, so check the result right after OK. Undo at once if an edge looks wrong. Stacking more changes on a bad frame makes the file harder to fix.
Edge cases when the file has several layers

Canvas Size applies to the whole document. Every layer gets the new frame, and its position stays tied to the anchor you chose. Check text, logos and shapes near the edges, because they can end up closer to the new border than you expect.
What to do next

Save a copy before you change the canvas on an important file. Use File > Save As, so the original keeps its size. If your menus differ from these steps, [update Photoshop](/how-to/update-photoshop-in-photoshop) first, then try again.
For a daily Photoshop routine on Mac, the [Photoshop page for designers](/for/designers/photoshop) covers shortcuts and a typical workflow.

faq.question: Does Canvas Size reduce image quality?
faq.answer: Not by itself. Canvas Size changes the frame, and the pixels inside keep their size. Image Size is the command that scales the pixels, so use it only when you want the photo itself bigger or smaller.

faq.question: What is the Canvas Size shortcut on Mac?
faq.answer: Most guides give Option+Command+C, shown as ⌥⌘C. One guide updated in September 2022 gives Shift+Command+C. Check the Image menu, where Photoshop prints the shortcut beside the command.

faq.question: Why is the canvas extension color greyed out?
faq.answer: The image has no Background layer. Use Layer > New > Background from Layer, then open Canvas Size again. One Adobe Community reply recommends this fix, but the original poster disputed it, so check the result.

faq.question: Can I change canvas size in Photoshop on the web?
faq.answer: Not with a dedicated command, according to a November 2023 Adobe Community answer. Use the Crop tool under Size & position, then drag the handles or type width and height values.

faq.question: Will shrinking the canvas delete my pixels?
faq.answer: The edges fall outside the frame and get cut. Photoshop warns you first, with Proceed, Learn More and Cancel. Save a copy first, or use the Crop tool with Delete Cropped Pixels unticked to keep them.

faq.question: Why does my photo look stretched after I changed the size?
faq.answer: You probably used Image Size instead of Canvas Size. Undo the change with Edit > Undo, then run Image > Canvas Size to set the new frame.

faq.question: Does the same command exist on Windows?
faq.answer: Yes. PhotoshopBuzz describes Image > Canvas Size in Photoshop CC for Windows. This page covers the Mac side, and the Windows shortcut is not covered here.

faq.question: Which Photoshop version do I need for this?
faq.answer: Adobe release coverage lists macOS 14.0 or later for Photoshop 27.0 and 27.6. The steps come from third-party guides, so check your build with the version guide linked earlier on this page.

task: Change canvas size in Photoshop on Mac
appliesTo: Photoshop 27.x on macOS 14.0 or later, with notes for older builds that share the Image menu
requirements: Photoshop desktop app for Mac, not the web app, for the full Canvas Size dialog
macOS 14.0 or later for Photoshop 27.0 and 27.6
A file open in Photoshop, with the Layers panel visible
A target size in mind, in pixels or a print unit

steps.name: Open the file and check the Background layer
steps.text: Open your file with File > Open, or drag it into Photoshop. Then open Window > Layers so you can see the layer stack. Look for a layer named Background with a small lock icon. You will need that check for transparent borders and color fills.

steps.name: Open the Canvas Size dialog
steps.text: Go to Image > Canvas Size. You can also press Option+Command+C. Some guides list Shift+Command+C instead. That conflicts with the rest, so if a shortcut does nothing, use the menu.

steps.name: Choose a unit before you type numbers
steps.text: Open the unit dropdown beside Width and Height. The options are Percent, Pixels, Centimeters and Millimeters. Pick the unit first, then type your numbers. That keeps the result easy to check against your plan.

steps.name: Enter the final width and height
steps.text: Type the new Width and Height. With Relative unticked, the numbers set the exact final size. Tick Relative only when you want to add or subtract a set amount from the current size.

steps.name: Pick an anchor square
steps.text: The nine-square grid sets where the image sits inside the new frame. The middle square adds space evenly on all sides. A corner or edge square keeps the image on that side, so the new space lands on the opposite sides.

steps.name: Choose the extension color
steps.text: Canvas extension color offers White, which is the default, plus Grey, Black and Other. The new area takes this color. If the option is greyed out, the image has no Background layer. The fix is in the section on greyed-out color above.

steps.name: Click OK and read any warning
steps.text: Canvas Size does not preview the change, so the first real look comes after OK. If you shrink the canvas, Photoshop warns that content will be clipped. Choose Proceed to continue, Learn More for details, or Cancel to stop.

steps.name: Check the edges and the proportions
steps.text: Look at each edge of the photo and the new area. If faces or products look stretched, you probably used Image Size. Undo the change with Edit > Undo, then run Canvas Size again.

steps.name: Save a copy
steps.text: Use File > Save As to keep the new canvas in a separate file. The original keeps its old frame, so you can go back if the new size does not work for the layout.

troubleshooting.problem: Canvas extension color is greyed out
troubleshooting.fix: The image has no Background layer. Use Layer > New > Background from Layer, then open Canvas Size again.

troubleshooting.problem: The photo looks stretched or squashed
troubleshooting.fix: You used Image Size. Undo with Edit > Undo, then use Image > Canvas Size instead.

troubleshooting.problem: The Crop tool fills the new area with odd patches
troubleshooting.fix: Content-Aware is selected. Deselect Content-Aware Fill in the options bar, then extend the canvas again.

troubleshooting.problem: Transparent border shows white or a solid color
troubleshooting.fix: The Background layer is locked. Click its lock icon in the Layers panel, then run Canvas Size again and check for the checkerboard pattern.

troubleshooting.problem: Edges disappeared after shrinking the canvas
troubleshooting.fix: Undo the change. Next time, save a copy first, or use the Crop tool with Delete Cropped Pixels unticked.
Use Image > Canvas Size from the menu. The shortcut printed in your build is more reliable than any guide, this one included.
